entries.clue: Doctor told lab nothing will come from it (3,4)

indicatorNotes.Doctor: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters get rearranged

blocks.note: anagram indicator
anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A physician is told the lab work will turn up nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' sits at the front looking like the subject of the sentence, but it is the instruction. A dot ball is cricket: a delivery off which no runs are scored, marked as a dot in the scorebook.
annotation.definitionFit: A dot ball yields nothing: no runs come from that delivery.

entries.clue: Want to accommodate Charlie round town, OK? (6)

indicatorNotes.to accommodate: the word takes Charlie in as a guest
indicatorNotes.round: turning something round writes it backwards

blocks.note: want = need
C in the NATO alphabet, set inside NEED to make NECED, then turned round
t = town, a map abbreviation

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a town is fine with putting up a visitor called Charlie.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' belongs with the want-and-Charlie unit before TOWN is added, not with 'town'.
annotation.definitionFit: Decent and OK both mean acceptable, good enough.

entries.clue: What often awaits you at A&E? Visit with no parking taking a very long time (6)

annotation.definition: What often awaits you at A&E?

indicatorNotes.with no: the word has to go without the letter named

blocks.note: TRIP (a visit) without P (parking)
an age = a very long time

annotation.surface: A grumble about hospital emergency visits that take forever with nowhere to park.
annotation.walkthrough: A&E (Accident and Emergency) is the British name for a hospital emergency room. The question mark flags the definition as a description rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Triage is the sorting of patients by urgency that meets you on arrival at an emergency department.

entries.clue: Reverses, so doing showing hesitation (5-5)

blocks.note: the verb: changes direction completely, as a soldier on parade does
'so doing' means doing what the answer describes; the result is a hesitation noise, ER

annotation.surface: Someone backtracking and dithering at the same time.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is a cryptic reading of the answer itself: ABOUT TURNS read as an instruction. Take 'about' as RE, turn it, and you get ER, the noise of someone hesitating.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the parade ground: to reverse direction is to turn about, and a U-turn in policy is called the same.

entries.clue: ‘Stick with it!’ Fail occasionally getting upset (5)

indicatorNotes.occasionally: only now and then, so every other letter
indicatorNotes.getting upset: upset in a down clue tips the letters upside down, reading them bottom to top

blocks.note: the even letters of wItH iT
the even letters of fAiL, continuing the same run

annotation.surface: An exhortation to persevere, from someone who fails now and then and gets upset about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick with it!' reads as one phrase, but only 'Stick' is the definition; 'with it' is fodder for the alternate letters. A lathi is a heavy bamboo stick used by Indian police.
annotation.definitionFit: A loanword from Hindi: the long iron-bound bamboo club carried by police in South Asia is simply a stick.

entries.clue: Corporate body running risk over start of enquiry – revealing these? (7)

indicatorNotes.running: running as in operating: the letters are set going in new order

blocks.note: the Post Office, a corporate body
anagram fodder
first letter of enquiry, placed after RISK before the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: An organisation taking risks just as an inquiry begins, and what the inquiry might expose.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the Post Office Horizon scandal and its public inquiry. Porkies is Cockney rhyming slang: pork pies = lies.
annotation.definitionFit: 'These' points back at what an enquiry into a corporate body might reveal: porkies, lies.

entries.clue: Following bad feeling second intervenes quickly (4-5)

indicatorNotes.intervenes: to intervene is to come between, so S goes into the middle of HATE

blocks.note: post = after, as in post-war
hate = bad feeling
s = second, inserted into HATE to make HASTE

annotation.surface: After an argument, a second person steps in fast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' opens the clue and looks like a connective, but it supplies POST.
annotation.definitionFit: From old letters marked 'haste, post, haste' for the fastest courier, it became a plain synonym for quickly.

entries.clue: Train flier (4)

blocks.note: the railway, as in going somewhere by train
a bird: the corncrake is one of this marsh family

annotation.surface: A train that flies, or a flier on a train.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Train flier' reads as one fast express, but it is two separate definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Rail is the train system, and a rail is also a bird.

entries.clue: Why I went to Pizza Express for a starter? (8)

annotation.definition2: Why I went to Pizza Express

blocks.clueFragment: Why I went to Pizza Express
blocks.note: a cryptic reading: the diner's reason for walking into a restaurant, said as four short words
a starter as a person, a beginner, not a first course

annotation.surface: A diner asking why they went to Pizza Express just for a starter.
annotation.walkthrough: Pizza Express is a British restaurant chain. The question it answers is not about the food: split the answer as IN IT I ATE. 'Starter' misleads towards the first course; here it means a beginner.
annotation.definitionFit: An initiate is a newcomer just admitted to something, so a starter in the sense of beginner.

entries.clue: Grating a lot of cheese, cry after mishap (8)

indicatorNotes.a lot of: most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes
indicatorNotes.after mishap: after a mishap the letters are in a mess

blocks.note: CHEESE without its last letter
anagram fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone grates too much cheese and yells after an accident with the grater.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grating' looks like the kitchen action on the cheese, but it is the definition, meaning harsh on the ear.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a grating voice is harsh and shrill, the quality of a screech.

entries.clue: Punch’s old material (5)

blocks.note: to chin someone is to punch them on the chin; the ’s reads as 'has' and joins
o = old, as in OT

annotation.surface: A question about the fabric of Mr Punch's old costume.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Punch’s' suggests the puppet of Punch and Judy, but it is a verb in disguise.
annotation.definitionFit: Chino is a twilled cotton cloth, the fabric of chinos.

entries.clue: Dummy trial for Trump rejected witness (9)

indicatorNotes.for: one thing stands in for another
indicatorNotes.rejected: sent back, so the letters are written in reverse

blocks.note: the American word for a baby's dummy
trial = test, which replaces PAC
to trump = to cap (outdo); CAP written backwards is PAC, removed from PACIFIER

annotation.surface: A mock trial staged for Donald Trump throws out a witness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trump' is not the president but the verb to outdo, which is CAP. A dummy is British for the rubber teat given to a baby, which Americans call a pacifier.
annotation.definitionFit: A testifier is someone who gives evidence, a witness.

entries.clue: Easy to pick up, Sir said previously (one’s not very bright) (5-5)

indicatorNotes.said: spoken, so what matters is the sound

blocks.note: a knight is addressed as Sir; KNIGHT sounds like NIGHT
light = not heavy, easy to lift

annotation.surface: A teacher's aside about a pupil who is quick to learn yet not very bright.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Previously' puts the Sir part first although it comes second in the clue. 'Not very bright' sounds like a dig at a person; it is literal, a dim lamp.
annotation.definitionFit: A night-light is a dim lamp left on overnight, so one not very bright.

entries.clue: Point to neat gin – it’s wrong drink for test (4,7)

indicatorNotes.wrong: the letters are in the wrong order

blocks.note: W = west, a compass point
anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone points out that neat gin is the wrong thing to drink before an exam.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 28 across. 'Test' suggests an exam, but the test here is of the wine.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the event is a drinking session whose purpose is to judge the wines.

entries.clue: Promises to provide funding for archaeologist’s work upfront – that’s great (10)

indicatorNotes.upfront: these pieces go at the front, before the promises

blocks.note: pro = for, in favour of
an excavation
IOUs are written promises to pay

annotation.surface: Someone thrilled at pledges of money for an archaeological dig paid in advance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upfront' reads as money paid in advance; it moves PRO and DIG ahead of the IOUS.
annotation.definitionFit: Prodigious means enormous or remarkable, great.

entries.clue: Preceding score no more than satisfactory (2,2,7)

blocks.note: up to = before, preceding
to score a surface is to scratch it

annotation.surface: A verdict on a result that was only passable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Score' sounds like a result or twenty; here it is the verb to mark a surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Up to scratch means meeting the required standard and no more.

entries.clue: ‘So, about young woman on the internet?’ (Think she may be getting suspicious) (3,6)

indicatorNotes.about: about in its sense of around, so the outer word goes round the inner one

blocks.note: so = thus; it goes around the young woman
e- for online plus MISS, a young woman

annotation.surface: A husband wonders whether his wife suspects his online chats with a young woman.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the 'she' of the parenthesis: the wife whose suspicion the surface fears. The rest of the bracket fills in the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: The missus is a colloquial term for one's wife, the 'she' who may be growing suspicious.

entries.clue: Caught in Scotland, maybe the biggest city in the country (8)

annotation.definition: the biggest city in the country

indicatorNotes.in: 'caught in' says the catch is held inside something else, so C sits within the other letters

blocks.note: c = caught, the cricket scorebook abbreviation
a land of auks, the seabirds of Scottish cliffs; C goes inside AUK

annotation.surface: A tip that the country's biggest city could be in Scotland.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The country' has no name in the clue, so it floats: Auckland is New Zealand's biggest city. 'Maybe' marks Scotland as an example of an auk land, not a definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Auckland is the largest city in New Zealand.

entries.clue: Prevents originally one motelier having sex (8)

indicatorNotes.having: having as in holding: the motelier holds the sex within him, so VI goes inside BATES

blocks.note: first letter of one
Norman Bates, who runs the motel in Psycho
sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals; it goes inside BATES

annotation.surface: A motel owner prevents something from happening in one of his rooms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sex' is Latin for six, not the act the motel surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: To obviate something is to prevent it or make it unnecessary.

entries.clue: Timeless Punjabi superstar being fanciful? It won’t be true (5,6)

indicatorNotes.Timeless: less means without, and time is T, so the phrase that follows drops a T

blocks.note: TURBAN, the headwear of a Sikh Punjabi star, without T (time)
a legend = a superstar
flags that 'turban legend' is a whimsical description, not a real phrase

annotation.surface: A celebrated Punjabi star whose fame may be exaggerated.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'turban legend' as a playful description of a Sikh Punjabi celebrity, not a real phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: An urban legend is a widely told story that is not true.

entries.clue: Threatened horny individual, one bothering a girl (6)

indicatorNotes.bothering: a bothered thing is disturbed, so the letters are stirred

blocks.note: a = one
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A randy man, menacing and pestering a girl.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Horny' is literal, as in having horns, and 'threatened' means endangered. The argali is a wild mountain sheep of Central Asia with huge curled horns.
annotation.definitionFit: The argali is a near-threatened wild sheep with enormous horns.

entries.clue: Pop up in bookies’ enclosure? (6)

blocks.note: SP = starting price, the bookmakers' odds when a race begins
the ring is the bookmakers' area at a racecourse

annotation.surface: Someone appearing suddenly in the betting area at the races.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pop up' reads as appear, and spring up is the sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: things that appear suddenly are said to spring up, and a jack-in-the-box both pops and springs.

entries.clue: Come together shouting ‘Booby!’ (4)

indicatorNotes.shouting: a word shouted is heard, not seen

blocks.note: a booby is a fool, a nit

annotation.surface: A crowd rallying while yelling insults.
annotation.walkthrough: Nit is British slang for a fool. 'Come together' is the way broken bones knit.
annotation.definitionFit: Broken bones knit, coming together as they heal.

entries.clue: Pricing rod for ‘guidance’ – it may be used for beating (6,4)

annotation.definition: it may be used for beating

indicatorNotes.guidance: the letters are guided into a new arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A pointer used to set prices, with a hint that it could also be used to hit someone.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'guidance' hint that the rearranging is its real job. A riding crop is a short whip for a horse.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by use: a jockey's short whip exists to strike the horse, and the surface's pointer hints the same.

entries.clue: Not the done thing to sleep through it (5)

indicatorNotes.through: NAP goes right through the middle of IT

blocks.note: it, taken as it is
a nap = a short sleep, placed inside IT

annotation.surface: Etiquette advice: snoozing through something is bad manners.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one plain sentence about manners, and the answer describes that very thing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something inappropriate or unsuitable to the occasion is not the done thing.

entries.clue: Content to clear Zulu fighters (4)

indicatorNotes.Content: the content of a word is its inside, without the outer letters

blocks.note: LIMPID (clear) without its outer letters

annotation.surface: Zulu warriors happy to clear out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as happy; it is the inside of the next word's synonym. An impi is a Zulu regiment.
annotation.definitionFit: A Zulu word for an armed regiment, so a specialist term that names the fighters themselves.

entries.clue: Herb Alpert releasing record – aim is to get hit (9)

indicatorNotes.releasing: letting go of the letters of the record
indicatorNotes.to get hit: the letters take a beating and land in a new order

anagram fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.walkthrough: 'Herb Alpert' reads as the bandleader's full name, but 'Herb' is the definition. A 'hit' record sounds like success; here hit means knocked about.
annotation.definitionFit: Artemisia is a genus of aromatic herbs including wormwood and tarragon.

entries.clue: Arab returning very soon (5)

blocks.note: in a mo(ment) = very soon

annotation.surface: An Arab coming back shortly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returning very soon' reads as one phrase about the Arab's travel plans; 'returning' is the instruction and 'very soon' the fodder. Mo is short for moment.
annotation.definitionFit: An Omani is a person from Oman, an Arab country.

entries.clue: Badmouth teacher getting sack (7)

blocks.note: to dis = to insult
pupils address a female teacher as Miss

annotation.surface: A teacher fired for speaking ill of someone.

annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sack is informal for firing someone from a job.
